reference: Worked examples are illustrative, not measured project results. Check provider and framework version-specific behavior against the linked primary documentation.

questions.title: How do you calculate token probabilities at different temperatures?
questions.simple: Temperature changes how strongly a generator favors its highest-scoring next token. It changes sampling probabilities, not the model weights or the facts available to it.
questions.technical: For logits z_i and positive temperature T, p_i = exp(z_i/T) / sum_j exp(z_j/T). Subtract max(z/T) before exponentiating for numerical stability. With a fixed vocabulary and finite logits, higher T flattens the distribution. T=0 is normally implemented as a greedy-decoding convention; directly dividing by zero is undefined. Provider support and interactions with other sampling controls vary.
questions.example: For the same logits [2,1,0], the leading token has probability about 66.5% at T=1, 50.6% at T=2 and 86.7% at T=0.5. Low temperature makes this particular choice more concentrated, but an incorrect high-logit token can still win.
followups: Does temperature zero guarantee repeatable or correct answers?
No. Greedy selection concerns decoding. Model updates, floating-point execution, ties, tools and changing context can alter outputs; correctness still needs evidence and evaluation.
When can a higher temperature help?
It can diversify brainstorming candidates. Evaluate candidate quality and downstream selection instead of assuming diversity is accuracy. Use stronger constraints for deterministic business outputs.

quiz.prompt: With logits [2,1,0], increasing temperature from 1 to 2 changes the highest token probability approximately how?
options: From 0.665 to 0.506; the distribution becomes flatter.
From 0.665 to 0.867; it becomes sharper.
It stays 0.665 because logits never change.
It becomes exactly 1 and eliminates hallucination.

questions.title: Calculate one scaled dot-product attention output using Q, K and V.
questions.simple: A query asks what information is useful, keys describe what each token offers, and values contain the information to mix. Attention compares the query with keys and forms a weighted average of values.
questions.technical: For one head, Q=XW_Q, K=XW_K and V=XW_V in self-attention. Compute scores QK^T/sqrt(d_k), apply any mask before row-wise softmax, then multiply by V. Cross-attention takes queries from a different stream than keys and values. Attention weights are input-dependent routing coefficients; they are not the trained W matrices.
questions.example: The first key matches the query more strongly, so its value gets about 67% of the weight. The output is 0.6698*[10,0] + 0.3302*[0,20], not a selection of only one value. This toy calculation omits dropout, output projection and other heads.
followups: Why divide by sqrt(d_k)?
For components with roughly unit variance, an unscaled dot product's variance grows with d_k. Scaling helps avoid overly large scores that saturate softmax and weaken useful gradients.
Are Q, K and V always identical?

No. They can start from the same token representations in self-attention but use distinct learned projections. Cross-attention uses different input streams, and architectures can share some projections deliberately.

quiz.prompt: For scores [0.7071,0] and values [10,0], [0,20], what is the approximate attention output?
options: [6.70,6.60], using softmax weights near [0.67,0.33].
[10,20], because attention concatenates both values.
[0.7071,0], because values are ignored.
[1,0], because attention must return the query.

questions.title: What are the matrix shapes and parameter counts in multi-head attention?
questions.simple: Each head examines a smaller representation of every token. The heads run side by side and their outputs are combined back into the model's hidden width.
questions.technical: For batch B, sequence length n, model width d and h equal-size standard heads, Q,K,V after projection can be reshaped to [B,h,n,d/h]. The attention score tensor is [B,h,n,n]. Concatenation returns [B,n,d], followed by an output projection. Standard full-width Q,K,V and output matrices contain approximately 4*d*d weights, excluding biases. GQA and MQA change key/value projection and cache sizes.
questions.formula:
B=2; n=128; d_model=512; heads=8; d_k=64
Q shape: [2,8,128,64]
attention scores: [2,8,128,128]
projection weights: 4*512*512 = 1,048,576
questions.example: Eight heads of width 64 still cover a total width of 512; they do not make the model width 4096. A 512-by-512 projection has 262,144 weights. Count all four projections separately and clarify whether the architecture uses shared K/V heads.
followups: What grows quadratically with sequence length?

The dense attention score/probability structure has n-by-n interactions per head. Optimized kernels avoid materializing the full matrix but do not make ordinary dense attention interaction count linear.
Does increasing head count at fixed width always increase parameters?
Not in standard full-width projections: the partitioning changes while the four d-by-d matrices remain. Other architectural choices and per-head overhead can change the result.

quiz.prompt: With d_model=512 and 8 standard heads, what is each head's key dimension?
options: 64, assuming equal head widths.
4096, because dimensions multiply by head count.
512 for each head, necessarily.
8, because head count equals key width.

questions.title: How do causal masking, KV caching, prefill and decoding fit together?
questions.simple: During generation, a token must not see future tokens. The server processes the prompt first, then generates new tokens while reusing keys and values already computed for the prefix.
questions.technical: Causal masking adds negative infinity to disallowed attention scores before softmax. Prefill computes the prompt's representations and cache. Decode appends new token K/V entries and attends to permitted prefix positions. A rough cache footprint is 2*layers*batch*tokens*KV_heads*head_dim*bytes_per_element, excluding allocator overhead. Cache usage depends on actual serving architecture, not just model parameter count.
questions.formula:
KV bytes ~= 2*L*B*N*H_kv*D_head*bytes
L=32; B=1; N=4096; H_kv=8; D_head=128; bytes=2
KV ~= 536,870,912 bytes = 512 MiB
questions.example: The toy configuration above needs roughly 512 MiB for one request's raw KV entries. Doubling the sequence length doubles that estimate. GQA with eight KV heads can use less KV storage than 32 independent KV heads at the same head width.
followups: Does KV caching eliminate all compute for every generated token?
No. Each new token still traverses the network and attends to the prefix. The cache avoids recomputing the historical keys/values; attention bandwidth and growing context still matter.
Can arbitrary prompts share a prefix cache?
Only compatible, genuinely identical prefixes under the engine's rules. Enforce privacy/isolation and include model/adapter/version identity; similar-looking text is not sufficient.

quiz.prompt: In the example with 32 layers, 4096 tokens and 8 KV heads of width 128 in FP16, raw KV storage is about what?
options: 512 MiB for batch size one.
512 bytes regardless of token count.
The entire parameter file size exactly.
Zero because caching removes memory usage.

questions.title: How do top-p and top-k interact with temperature?
questions.simple: Temperature reshapes scores. Top-k keeps a fixed number of high-ranked candidates; top-p keeps a smallest high-ranked prefix whose probability mass reaches a chosen threshold.
questions.technical: Sampling implementations apply temperature and truncation in a particular order, then renormalize. Inspect the provider's semantics before deriving exact probabilities. Nucleus size varies by distribution. Increasing top-p permits a larger candidate set but does not itself train a more knowledgeable model. Simultaneously tuning several controls makes attribution difficult.
questions.example: For sorted probabilities [0.60,0.25,0.10,0.05], top-p=0.8 retains the first two tokens because their cumulative mass is 0.85. After renormalization their probabilities are about [0.706,0.294]. Top-k=3 would retain three candidates before any additional rules.
followups: Would top-p=0.8 keep exactly 80% of the vocabulary?
No. It is a probability-mass threshold, not a vocabulary percentage. A peaked distribution can cross it with one token.
Which control should you tune first?
Hold the other controls fixed, choose one based on the task, and compare on a versioned evaluation set. Provider restrictions can determine which settings are available.

quiz.prompt: For [0.60,0.25,0.10,0.05], which tokens does top-p=0.8 retain under the usual nucleus rule?
options: The first two, whose cumulative probability is 0.85.
All four because 0.8 exceeds every individual probability.
Exactly 80% of vocabulary entries.
Only the last token because it is least likely.

questions.title: Calculate cross-entropy and perplexity, and explain their limits.
questions.simple: Cross-entropy penalizes a model when it assigns low probability to the correct next token. Perplexity expresses average token uncertainty on an exponential scale.
questions.technical: For N evaluated target tokens, mean negative log-likelihood is -(1/N)*sum(log p(y_t|prefix)); perplexity is exp(mean NLL) when natural logarithms are used. Specify token masking, tokenizer, dataset and context. Lower perplexity on one distribution does not prove better factual accuracy, instruction following or tool safety, and scores across incompatible tokenizers are not directly comparable.
questions.example: A model that predicts two target tokens with probabilities 0.5 and 0.25 has perplexity about 2.83 on this toy sequence. This says nothing about whether a generated financial claim is supported by a source; that needs a separate grounded task evaluation.
followups: Why average logs rather than probabilities?
Sequence likelihood multiplies conditional probabilities. Logs turn the product into a stable sum and penalize confidently low probabilities on the correct targets.
Can a fluent hallucination have low perplexity?
Yes. Plausible language can be likely without being true for the user's case. Evaluate source support, correctness and abstention separately.

quiz.prompt: For target probabilities 0.5 and 0.25 using natural logs, what is perplexity?
options: About 2.83.
Exactly 0.375, their arithmetic mean.
Exactly 75% factual accuracy.
Zero, because both probabilities are positive.

questions.title: Scenario: Temperature zero still produces a confident wrong answer. How do you repair it?
questions.simple: Making the model less random does not give it missing facts or fix a misleading prompt. Trace whether the failure came from evidence, interpretation, reasoning or output handling.
questions.technical: Capture the exact model revision, prompt template, rendered context, token counts, retrieved IDs and output. Reproduce on a sanitized failing case. If evidence is absent, repair retrieval or abstain; if evidence is present, inspect truncation, conflicting instructions and constrained output handling. Test the repair on failure slices and a holdout before canary rollout.
questions.example: A refund bot says 30 days at T=0 because a stale 30-day policy dominates its context while the current policy says 14. Selecting greedily simply repeats the stale answer more consistently.
questions.architecture: Versioned request trace -> authorized evidence check -> prompt and token inspection -> targeted repair -> held-out evaluation -> canary and rollback
questions.metrics: Grounded answer correctness, unsupported-claim rate, abstention precision/recall, cohort regressions, latency and cost per successful request.
questions.tradeoffs: Adding a verifier introduces latency and can miss errors. Prefer authoritative evidence and deterministic business checks where possible; a second model is not a guarantee.
followups: Should you increase temperature until it says 14?
No. That selects a lucky sample rather than fixing the causal failure. Repair the evidence/decision boundary and evaluate repeated runs as appropriate.
When would fine-tuning help?
For repeatable behavior or domain task patterns with representative training data. Frequently changing factual policy is usually better supplied through governed retrieval or an authoritative API.

quiz.prompt: A greedy decoder repeatedly quotes an expired policy. What is the best first repair?
options: Verify source applicability and the rendered context before changing sampling.
Raise temperature until a desired answer appears.
Add GPU replicas without inspecting evidence.
Declare temperature zero a factuality guarantee.

questions.title: What are mean, median, variance and standard deviation?
questions.simple: Mean is the arithmetic average; median is the middle value. Variance measures squared spread around the mean, and standard deviation brings spread back to the original units.
questions.technical: For independent observations, the usual sample variance divides squared deviations by n-1 to estimate population variance under its assumptions. Population variance divides by n. Median resists isolated extremes more than mean. Heavy tails and multimodal data require distribution inspection rather than reporting one summary alone.
questions.example: For [1,2,3,4,100], mean=22 and median=3. The mean is pulled toward the extreme value. If these are legitimate transaction amounts, changing 100 to 4 silently destroys real business information.
followups: Is median always the best imputation?
No. It is a robust baseline for skewed numeric features, but missingness patterns, feature meaning and model behavior matter. Fit it within the training fold.
Does standard deviation assume data is normal?
It can be calculated without normality. Interpreting fixed sigma ranges as particular coverage probabilities requires distributional assumptions.

quiz.prompt: For [1,2,3,4,100], what are the mean and median?
options: Mean 22, median 3.
Mean 3, median 22.
Both 22 because outliers are ignored.
Both 100 because it is the maximum.

questions.title: What are the central limit theorem and the law of large numbers?
questions.simple: The law of large numbers concerns an average settling toward its expected value. A central limit theorem concerns the distribution of a suitably scaled average around that value.
questions.technical: In the classic independent identically distributed finite-variance setting, sqrt(n)*(sample_mean-mu)/sigma converges in distribution to a standard normal. This does not make the raw data normal. Dependence, selection bias and heavy tails can undermine naive normal intervals; there is no universal n=30 guarantee.
questions.example: Purchase amounts may stay strongly right-skewed, while means from many sufficiently large independent samples become approximately normal. Sampling only premium customers still estimates the wrong population even with a million rows.
followups: Does more data remove sampling bias?
No. Large biased samples can estimate the wrong population very precisely. Inspect coverage, selection and the deployment population.
What if records belong to the same customer?
They may be dependent. Use group-aware estimation/splitting and an uncertainty method suited to the sampling unit, such as a cluster bootstrap when justified.

quiz.prompt: What does a classic central limit theorem say becomes approximately normal under its assumptions?
options: The standardized sampling distribution of the mean.
Every individual raw observation.
Any biased dataset after exactly 30 rows.
The classification labels themselves.

questions.title: What is Bayes' theorem, and why does base rate matter?
questions.simple: Bayes' theorem updates a prior belief using observed evidence. A seemingly strong detector can still produce many false alarms when the event is rare.
questions.technical: P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). Positive predictive value depends on sensitivity, specificity and prevalence. A model's recall alone does not determine how trustworthy a positive prediction is. Estimate using deployment-like base rates and account for uncertainty or changing prevalence.
questions.formula:
P(fraud|alert) = TP/(TP+FP)
10,000 cases; 1% fraud; recall=90%; FPR=5%
TP=90; FP=495; precision=90/585=15.38%
questions.example: The detector finds 90 of 100 frauds but also flags 495 legitimate cases. Only about 15.4% of its alerts are fraud. This illustrative arithmetic explains why an analyst queue can be overwhelmed despite high recall.
followups: Can balanced-test precision predict production precision?
Not directly when prevalence differs. Reweight or evaluate a representative sample and report the assumed base rate.
Should you optimize only recall?
No. Choose a threshold using missed-event cost, false-alarm burden, capacity and policy constraints. Show the trade-off curve rather than a single unsupported target.

quiz.prompt: Among 90 true-positive alerts and 495 false-positive alerts, what is precision?
options: 90%, because recall is 90%.
99%, because most cases are legitimate.

questions.title: Calculate precision, recall, F1, specificity and accuracy from a confusion matrix.
questions.simple: Each metric asks a different question: whether alerts are reliable, whether positives are found, whether negatives are rejected, or how often all predictions match.
questions.technical: TP=positive predicted positive; FP=negative predicted positive; FN=positive predicted negative; TN=negative predicted negative. Precision=TP/(TP+FP), recall=TP/(TP+FN), specificity=TN/(TN+FP), F1=2TP/(2TP+FP+FN), accuracy=(TP+TN)/N. Declare positive class, averaging and handling of zero denominators.
questions.example: The model is 97% accurate yet misses one-third of positives. If positives are critical equipment failures, the 97% headline hides a costly recall problem. Use business-sensitive error analysis rather than comparing headline accuracy alone.
followups: When do micro and macro averages differ?

Macro averages per-class scores equally; micro pools counts, favoring common classes. For single-label multiclass classification, micro F1 equals accuracy, so minority recall needs separate reporting.
Does F1 include true negatives?
No. Its formula uses TP, FP and FN. It does not measure calibration, true-negative burden or every business cost.

quiz.prompt: With TP=40, FP=10 and FN=20, what is F1?
options: 80/110, approximately 0.727.
0.97 because that is overall accuracy.
40/50, exactly precision.
40/60, exactly recall.

questions.title: Calculate a gradient descent update for linear regression.
questions.simple: Gradient descent changes a weight a little in the direction that lowers the chosen loss. Learning rate controls the step size.
questions.technical: For one sample, prediction wx+b and loss (1/2)*(prediction-y)^2 give gradients (prediction-y)*x and (prediction-y). Update both using gradients evaluated at the old parameters. Batch averaging, loss scaling and optimizer state change exact numerical updates; state your convention before calculating.
questions.formula:
x=2; y=5; w=1; b=0; learning_rate=0.1
prediction=2; error=-3
dL/dw=-6; dL/db=-3
w_new=1-0.1*(-6)=1.6; b_new=0.3
questions.example: With new w=1.6 and b=0.3, the same sample predicts 3.5, closer to 5. One improving sample update does not establish generalization; check training dynamics and validation performance.
followups: What if the loss omits the one-half?
Both gradients gain a factor of two. Equivalent learning-rate scaling can compensate, but the written formula must match the calculation.
Why can a very large learning rate diverge?
The step can overshoot a low-loss region and amplify errors. Inspect scaling, gradients and schedules rather than assuming more steps always help.

quiz.prompt: For half-squared loss with x=2,y=5,w=1,b=0 and learning rate 0.1, what is the simultaneous update?
options: w=6 and b=3.
w stays 1 because linear regression has no gradient.

questions.title: How do bagging, boosting and stacking differ?
questions.simple: Bagging combines models trained on varied samples; boosting builds models that improve a running ensemble; stacking trains another model to combine base predictions.
questions.technical: Random forests combine bootstrapped trees and random feature subsets to reduce correlated variance. Gradient boosting fits successive learners to a loss-related negative-gradient target. A stacker must train on out-of-fold base predictions to avoid leakage. Ensemble choice depends on data size, noise, latency, interpretability and deployment constraints.
questions.example: If a base model's training predictions feed a stacker, the stacker sees unrealistically easy inputs. Generate predictions from folds where that row was not used to fit the base model, then train the meta-model on those predictions.
followups: Is boosting always better on noisy labels?
No. Excessive capacity or iterations can fit noise. Tune regularization and early stopping with suitable validation and investigate label quality.
Does adding more trees always reduce latency?
No. Serving cost can grow with ensemble size. Measure prediction latency, memory and quality at the chosen configuration.

quiz.prompt: What should train a stacking meta-model to reduce leakage?
options: Out-of-fold predictions from the base models.
Only base predictions on the same rows each base model fit.
The final test labels during feature engineering.
Random labels to guarantee independence.

questions.title: What is probability calibration, and how do Platt scaling and isotonic regression help?
questions.simple: A calibrated model's 80% predictions should be correct about 80% of the time over comparable cases. Ranking quality and trustworthy probability values are different properties.
questions.technical: Sigmoid/Platt-style calibration fits a parametric mapping; isotonic fits a nondecreasing flexible mapping and usually needs more calibration data. Fit calibration on held-out or cross-validated predictions, not the same overfit training outputs. Assess reliability plots and proper scoring rules such as log loss or Brier score with subgroup and sample-size checks.
questions.example: A credit-risk model ranks cases well but outcomes occur in only 40% of cases scored near 0.8. A threshold based on the raw probabilities can misprice risk even if ROC-AUC looks strong. Calibrate and evaluate on deployment-like cases.
followups: Can calibration preserve ranking?
Monotone mappings generally preserve ordering, though ties can be introduced. Calibration and discrimination should still be reported separately.
Can you calibrate once forever?
No. Changes in prevalence, feature distribution or the base model can break the mapping. Monitor reliability and recalibrate using suitable new labeled data.

quiz.prompt: A model has high AUC but its 0.8 predictions succeed only 40% of the time. What is wrong?
options: Its probability calibration is poor despite useful ranking.
Its ranking must necessarily be random.
Its accuracy must be exactly 80%.
Temperature alone proves the business risk is correct.

questions.title: What are permutation importance and SHAP, and can they prove causality?
questions.simple: Feature importance explains aspects of a model's predictions, not necessarily what would happen if the world were changed. Correlated features can share or hide importance.
questions.technical: Permutation importance measures score degradation after disrupting a feature on representative evaluation data. SHAP attributes a prediction relative to a background/reference distribution under chosen dependence assumptions. Correlation, leakage and unstable data can distort interpretation. Use held-out performance, subgroup checks and domain review; causal intervention claims require separate assumptions and evidence.
questions.example: Both postcode and income correlate with loan outcomes. Shuffling postcode while leaving correlated features intact may understate its joint information, while the model can still encode sensitive proxies. A small reported importance is not a fairness certificate.
followups: Should you calculate importance on training data only?
No. Held-out evaluation helps distinguish generalizable use from overfit patterns. Document the chosen data distribution and scoring metric.
Can SHAP justify rejecting a customer automatically?
It is an explanatory aid, not proof of policy validity or causal fairness. Decisions need appropriate governance, error review and the applicable business process.

quiz.prompt: What can a SHAP attribution establish on its own?
options: An explanation of a model prediction relative to stated background assumptions.
A causal effect of changing the feature in the real world.
A guarantee of fairness across all groups.
Proof that the training labels are correct.

questions.title: How do class weights, undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE differ?
questions.simple: These methods change how much rare classes influence learning. They do not create trustworthy labels or remove the need for representative evaluation.
questions.technical: Class weights modify the loss; undersampling discards some majority examples; oversampling repeats or synthesizes minority examples. SMOTE interpolates in a feature neighborhood and can be inappropriate for categorical, temporal or constrained features without a suitable method. Apply resampling only inside training folds, then evaluate on untouched deployment-like data and calibrate if needed.
questions.example: If you synthesize examples before splitting, related real/synthetic points can enter both train and test. This leaks information and inflates metrics. A pipeline should split first and fit resampling only on each training fold.
followups: Does a 50:50 training set mean production precision is measured at 50:50?
No. Report evaluation at the real or explicitly modeled deployment base rate. Training prevalence and deployment prevalence have different purposes.
When is undersampling dangerous?
When it removes important majority subgroups or rare legitimate behavior. Compare subgroup errors and retain representative difficult negatives.

quiz.prompt: Where should SMOTE run during cross-validation?
options: Inside each training fold only.
On the full dataset before making folds.
On the test labels to balance the final score.
On production traffic with no labels or validation.

questions.title: What is DBSCAN, and how does it differ from K-means?
questions.simple: K-means assigns points to a chosen number of centroid-based groups. DBSCAN connects dense neighborhoods and can label isolated points as noise.
questions.technical: K-means minimizes within-cluster squared Euclidean distance and suits appropriately scaled compact clusters. DBSCAN uses eps and min_samples, handles some non-spherical shapes and does not require a cluster count, but varying density and high-dimensional distance concentration complicate tuning. Neither algorithm's clusters automatically correspond to meaningful business categories.
questions.example: Two crescent-shaped groups can be split poorly by a nearest-centroid boundary. A suitable DBSCAN neighborhood can follow the connected shapes, but one eps may fail when one group is much denser than the other.
followups: Is every DBSCAN noise point a fraud?
No. Noise means sparse under the chosen features and parameters. Validate business meaning and review false alarms.
How do you evaluate clustering without labels?
Use stability, domain utility and suitable internal metrics while checking their geometric assumptions. A high silhouette score is not proof of operational value.

quiz.prompt: Which property fits DBSCAN?
options: Density-connected groups with possible noise labels and no required cluster count.
A mandatory preset K and only spherical centroids.
A guarantee that every noise point is malicious.
No sensitivity to feature scaling or neighborhood parameters.

questions.title: Scenario: You must forecast demand with promotions, holidays and delayed labels. How do you validate?
questions.simple: Make each validation run imitate what was knowable at the time of prediction. Future sales, later corrections and revised promotional data must not leak backward.
questions.technical: Use rolling-origin splits, point-in-time feature joins and prediction-time availability rules. Fit imputation/scaling within each training window. Include naive seasonal baselines, demand segments, horizons and intermittent-demand cases. Distinguish labels unavailable yet from true zero sales. Set retraining and evaluation schedules around label delay.
questions.example: A feature computed from the final week's total sales cannot predict Monday of that same week. Instead, use a lagged window that ends before the forecast cutoff and promotion plans actually published by then.
questions.architecture: Timestamped events -> point-in-time features -> rolling-origin training -> horizon-specific forecasts -> delayed-label reconciliation -> monitored retraining
questions.metrics: MAE or suitable scaled error by horizon and item; bias, underforecast cost, stockout rate, coverage of intervals and error against seasonal baselines.
questions.tradeoffs: Frequent retraining can use immature labels. Rich global models share data but can hide poor performance on low-volume items; compare segment behavior and operational cost.
followups: Why not random train/test split?
Nearby time observations and future regime information can leak across the split, producing an optimistic estimate of future forecasting quality.
Why can MAPE fail here?
Zero or near-zero demand makes its denominator unstable or undefined. Choose metrics and business costs that remain meaningful for those items.

quiz.prompt: Which validation best matches a future demand forecasting task?
options: Rolling-origin splits with features available before each cutoff.
Randomly mix all dates and use final corrected future totals.
Fit preprocessing on all dates before validation.
Drop every zero-demand item to improve MAPE silently.

questions.title: Scenario: A model's average score improves but a small user group gets worse. Can you ship?
questions.simple: An average can hide harm to a minority group. Inspect the affected slice, measurement uncertainty and decision consequences before approving the release.
questions.technical: Define relevant cohorts and critical error budgets before release. Compare baseline and candidate on the same cases, examine sample size/confidence intervals and rule out data/label changes. Use stratified monitoring and human review where appropriate. A canary should have stop conditions for critical slices, not just global latency and accuracy.
questions.example: Overall recall rises from 85% to 88%, while recall for a small language cohort falls from 70% to 40%. The weighted average improves because most cases use another language; that does not resolve the regression.
questions.architecture: Versioned evaluation cases -> overall and cohort metrics -> uncertainty and failure review -> targeted repair -> guarded canary -> cohort-aware monitoring
questions.metrics: Recall/precision and calibration by cohort, sample counts, confidence intervals, severity-weighted error rate and coverage of abstention/review.
questions.tradeoffs: Tiny slices have noisy estimates; use targeted data collection and domain review. Do not either ignore the slice or declare significance from a handful of cases.
followups: Does equal accuracy prove fairness?
No. Error types, base rates, calibration, access and decision costs can differ. Choose metrics with domain and policy context.
What if the cohort is too small for a reliable estimate?
Report uncertainty, collect representative data and constrain rollout or route sensitive cases for review rather than inventing confidence.

quiz.prompt: A global metric improves while a critical cohort regresses sharply. What should decide rollout?
options: Cohort error budgets, uncertainty and consequences alongside overall results.
The global average alone.
Removing the cohort from evaluation.
Deploying everywhere to gather unbounded evidence of harm.

questions.title: Scenario: Training and serving produce different feature values. How do you find training-serving skew?
questions.simple: The model may receive different inputs in production even when its weights are unchanged. Compare feature definitions and point-in-time examples across both paths.
questions.technical: Trace raw inputs, schema versions, preprocessing artifacts, time windows, category handling and freshness. Replay sanitized production examples through the training transform and compare values before scoring. Share versioned transformation code or contracts and monitor missingness/range/distribution. Feature stores help consistency only if access, computation and timestamps are correct.
questions.example: Training divides amounts by 100 to convert cents to dollars; serving passes cents directly. A $20 purchase is seen as 2000 rather than 20. Scaling the API does not repair this deterministic feature bug.
questions.architecture: Versioned event schema -> shared validated transforms -> point-in-time replay comparison -> model scoring -> feature drift and freshness monitors
questions.metrics: Feature mismatch rate, schema rejection rate, freshness lag, null rates, score-distribution shift and delayed-label task quality.
questions.tradeoffs: Strict schema rejection can reduce availability. Define fail-open/fail-closed behavior by feature and business risk, with an explicit fallback model or manual process.
followups: Is all drift training-serving skew?
No. Skew is a mismatch in representation or pipeline semantics; population drift can occur even with identical transformations. Diagnose both.
Would retraining fix a unit-conversion bug?
It could conceal it temporarily but leaves an inconsistent contract. Correct the transform and validate affected predictions before retraining if needed.

quiz.prompt: Training uses dollars but serving sends cents. What is the main failure?
options: Training-serving feature skew caused by an inconsistent unit contract.
A necessary consequence of more data.
Insufficient model temperature.
A problem fixed solely by increasing class weights.

questions.title: S3, EBS and EFS: which storage fits which workload?
questions.simple: S3 stores objects through an API; EBS provides block volumes typically attached to EC2; EFS provides a managed shared file system. They expose different access and consistency interfaces.
questions.technical: Choose by object versus filesystem access, sharing needs, throughput, latency, AZ design and cost. An EBS volume is not a general multi-writer shared application database. EFS is not automatically the right database storage. S3 object keys are not POSIX file paths, and an object overwrite is not a transactional row update.
questions.example: Store uploaded manuals and immutable ingestion artifacts in S3. Put an EC2 database's storage on an appropriately designed block-storage setup. Use a shared file system only when the application genuinely needs compatible shared-file semantics.
followups: Can you keep a Netlify SQLite file in its deployment folder for durable shared users?
No. A serverless deployment's filesystem is not a shared durable database. Use a supported persistent database service; this app uses remote libSQL-compatible storage.
Does S3 remove the need for a metadata database?
No. Queryable workflow state, ownership and transactional constraints often belong in a database, while large immutable blobs remain in object storage.

quiz.prompt: Which storage is the usual fit for uploaded document objects accessed by key?
options: S3 object storage.
A browser's session cookie.
An EC2 instance's RAM only.
An SQS visibility timeout.

questions.title: What is a VPC endpoint, and how is it different from a NAT gateway?
questions.simple: A NAT gateway provides outbound connectivity for suitable private-subnet traffic. VPC endpoints offer service-specific private connectivity paths, depending on endpoint type and service support.
questions.technical: Gateway endpoints support particular services such as S3 and DynamoDB using route-table integration. Interface endpoints use private IPs and service-specific configuration. Compare regional support, DNS, endpoint policies, security groups where applicable, routing and cost. Neither endpoint selection nor private networking grants IAM permissions automatically.
questions.example: A worker reading a large S3 corpus may use an S3 gateway endpoint instead of routing that service traffic through NAT. It still needs an allowed IAM identity and compatible bucket policy.
followups: Does a private subnet guarantee no data exfiltration?
No. Egress routes, credentials, endpoints and application behavior determine reachable destinations and permitted actions.
Can an endpoint solve a denied S3 request?
Only if the issue is connectivity or an endpoint/bucket-policy boundary. IAM or encryption-key authorization failures require inspecting those policies too.

quiz.prompt: After adding an S3 VPC endpoint, what remains required?
options: Correct routing and explicit IAM/bucket-policy authorization.
No IAM policy because the network is private.
A public IP on every document.
Disabling all bucket encryption.

questions.title: What are readiness, liveness and load-balancer health checks?
questions.simple: Readiness asks whether a process should receive work; liveness asks whether it should be restarted. A load-balancer check controls which registered targets receive traffic under that balancer's rules.
questions.technical: Design checks around initialization, critical dependencies, draining and failure modes. A readiness failure should not necessarily trigger a restart storm. Container/orchestrator probes and ALB health checks are distinct mechanisms. Avoid making every replica restart just because a shared database is briefly unavailable.
questions.example: A model-serving container is alive while loading weights but not ready for inference. Route traffic only after a representative initialization check succeeds, then drain accepted streams before termination.
followups: Should liveness execute a costly full model inference every second?
Usually no. It can overload serving and cause false failures. Separate lightweight process health from readiness and periodic deeper synthetic checks.
What if all targets are unhealthy?
Inspect the actual load balancer's documented behavior and implement an explicit outage path. Do not assume health checks alone guarantee traffic is safely rejected.

quiz.prompt: A model process is running but still loading weights. Which status is appropriate?
options: Alive, but not ready to accept inference work.
Ready because a process ID exists.
Dead and requiring an infinite restart loop.
Authorized for every user because it started.

questions.title: SQS Standard versus FIFO: what does exactly-once language actually mean?
questions.simple: Standard queues can deliver duplicates. FIFO adds ordering within message groups and deduplication behavior, but a business action can still be repeated if your consumer's success is not safely recorded.
questions.technical: Design idempotent consumers with durable operation identities. FIFO deduplication and ordering have documented scope and limits; they do not atomically commit an external payment or document index update with queue acknowledgement. Visibility timeout, deletion and retry behavior remain operational concerns. Message group design affects parallelism.
questions.example: A worker charges an account and crashes before deleting the message. Redelivery must look up the same payment operation ID rather than create a second charge. Queue deduplication is not a substitute for business idempotency.
followups: Why can one FIFO message group become a bottleneck?
Ordering within that group limits concurrent progression. Partition groups by an appropriate ordering key without breaking the required business order.
Does a DLQ prove a message is permanently invalid?
No. It records exhausted delivery/processing attempts under a policy. Diagnose transient dependency issues, poison payloads and version mismatches before replay.

quiz.prompt: A FIFO worker performs a payment then crashes before acknowledgement. What protects against a duplicate payment?
options: Durable business idempotency tied to the same operation ID.
Assuming FIFO atomically commits the payment with deletion.
Generating a new payment ID on every retry.
Increasing the LLM temperature.

questions.title: How do you choose queue concurrency and estimate backlog drain time?
questions.simple: Consumers must process work faster than it arrives to shrink a backlog. More workers help only until a shared dependency becomes the bottleneck.
questions.technical: If arrival rate is lambda, sustainable service rate mu must exceed lambda. Approximate drain time for backlog B under steady rates is B/(mu-lambda). Estimate concurrency from measured service times and capacity constraints, not CPU alone. Backlog age, model quotas, database connections and fairness matter; workload variance makes simple averages optimistic.
questions.formula:
backlog=600 jobs; arrivals=10 jobs/s
processing=20 jobs/s
drain time ~= 600/(20-10) = 60 seconds
If processing <= arrivals, backlog does not drain.
questions.example: At two jobs per second per worker, ten workers nominally provide 20 jobs/s. A provider quota capped at 12 jobs/s changes the net drain rate to only 2 jobs/s, so the same backlog takes about 300 seconds under these assumptions.
followups: Why scale on oldest-message age?
It exposes user waiting time that queue length alone can hide. Combine age, arrival rate, service rate and failure/retry counts.
What if a small tenant floods the queue?
Apply per-tenant budgets, fair scheduling or partitioning and admission limits. Unlimited concurrency can amplify dependency throttling.

quiz.prompt: With 600 queued jobs, 10 jobs/s arriving and 20 jobs/s processed, approximate drain time is what?
options: 60 seconds under steady-rate assumptions.
30 seconds, ignoring new arrivals.
6000 seconds regardless of processing rate.
Zero because Auto Scaling always clears queues instantly.

questions.title: What are Step Functions retries, catches and workflow compensation?
questions.simple: An orchestrator records steps and routes failures. Retrying a step repeats work; compensation is a separate business action intended to address a completed effect.
questions.technical: Classify transient versus permanent errors and apply bounded backoff with jitter and a whole-workflow time budget. Persist operation identity across retries. A catch path can route to cleanup or human review, but does not automatically roll back remote services. Choose workflow/service modes based on documented execution, history, limits and cost.
questions.example: A report workflow reserves capacity, creates a document and emails a link. If email fails, deleting the document is not always the right compensation. The business may prefer retrying delivery or surfacing an incomplete-delivery status.
followups: Should validation errors be retried forever?
No. A deterministic invalid payload needs correction or a dead-letter/manual path. Repeating it consumes capacity without progress.
Can compensation perfectly undo every action?
No. A sent email or disclosed document cannot be unsent by deleting state. Model irreversibility explicitly.

quiz.prompt: A failed workflow step has already sent an email. What does a catch handler guarantee?
options: Only the configured failure path; it cannot automatically unsend the email.
Full rollback of every external effect.
Exactly-once execution of all downstream systems.
That no further monitoring is necessary.

questions.title: How do IAM identity policies, resource policies and explicit deny interact?
questions.simple: Authorization is evaluated across relevant policy boundaries. An explicit deny can block an action even when another policy appears to allow it.
questions.technical: Inspect the actual principal, assumed role session, action, resource, conditions and applicable policy types. Permissions boundaries, organization controls and service-specific rules can limit identity grants. Resource-based access and cross-account behavior need their own evaluation. Least privilege means a narrow documented action/resource set, not simply avoiding administrator names.
questions.example: A worker's identity policy allows s3:GetObject, but a bucket policy explicitly denies requests outside an approved network path. Adding another identity allow does not override that deny.
followups: Why prefer roles over embedding long-lived access keys?
Roles provide scoped temporary credentials through supported identity flows and reduce static-key distribution. Their trust and permission policies still require care.
Does KMS permission follow automatically from S3 read access?
Not necessarily. An encrypted object can require compatible key permissions and key policy. Inspect both the storage and encryption authorization paths.

quiz.prompt: An identity allow conflicts with an applicable explicit deny. What wins?
options: The explicit deny.
The policy with the longest text.
The identity allow always overrides all restrictions.
Whichever statement the LLM reads first.

questions.title: RDS Multi-AZ versus read replicas: which solves availability and which solves read scale?
questions.simple: Availability designs prepare for failures; replicas can serve additional reads under supported configurations. A copy of data is not automatically a backup or a strongly consistent read endpoint.
questions.technical: RDS deployment types differ: a traditional Multi-AZ instance standby is not a read-scaling target, while Multi-AZ DB clusters expose different readable-instance behavior. Read replicas generally have replication-lag and promotion considerations. Specify engine and deployment type, connection recovery, transaction semantics and RPO/RTO instead of saying all replicas behave identically.
questions.example: A recently completed purchase may not yet appear on an asynchronously replicated read target. Route read-after-write queries appropriately or design a user-visible eventual-consistency policy.
followups: Can a replica replace backups?
No. Logical deletion or corruption can replicate. Keep tested backups and restoration procedures with required retention and recovery objectives.
Why can more API replicas hurt RDS?
Each may open a connection pool. Total connections can exceed database capacity; bound pools, use suitable pooling/proxies and fix expensive queries.

quiz.prompt: Why might a read replica return an older value immediately after a write?
options: Replication lag can make the read eventually consistent.
Every replica is always synchronously identical by definition.
The database must be unencrypted.
Load balancing changes the committed transaction's value.

questions.title: Scenario: A Lambda and SQS pipeline repeats messages and overwhelms the model endpoint. What do you change?
questions.simple: Limit work to the model's capacity and make repeated messages safe. A queue absorbs bursts but cannot create unlimited downstream quota.
questions.technical: Measure invocation concurrency, batch behavior, timeouts, visibility, retry rate and provider throttle response. Cap event-source/worker concurrency, use per-operation idempotency, configure partial-batch failure handling where supported and route exhausted failures deliberately. Keep a total retry budget and admission policy; separate deterministic bad payloads from transient throttles.
questions.example: A batch contains nine successful jobs and one failed job. Repeating all ten without durable job IDs can duplicate nine effects. Correct partial-batch handling and idempotency reduce amplification.
questions.architecture: Admission limit -> SQS -> bounded Lambda consumers -> idempotency store -> quota-aware model calls -> result store and acknowledgement -> DLQ review
questions.metrics: Oldest message age, processing success rate, duplicate effects, model throttles, retries per success, concurrency and cost per completed job.
questions.tradeoffs: Lower concurrency can increase wait time but preserve useful throughput. Increase actual inference capacity or reject excess demand when the latency objective cannot be met.
followups: Should every timeout trigger a new job ID?
No. Preserve the original logical identity and reconcile unknown outcomes; a timeout does not prove no remote effect occurred.
What should happen before DLQ replay?
Classify the failure, repair the cause, preserve operation IDs and replay at bounded rate. Blind replay can recreate the outage.

quiz.prompt: A queued ingestion workload is throttling inference. What is the best first scaling boundary?
options: Bound consumer concurrency to measured downstream capacity and make retries idempotent.
Increase consumers without any cap or quota check.
Remove the queue and retry synchronously forever.
Generate a new operation ID for every delivery.

questions.title: Scenario: An application works locally but receives AccessDenied on AWS. How do you debug safely?
questions.simple: Identify the actual cloud identity and the specific denied action. Do not solve an unknown permission failure by granting administrator access.
questions.technical: Inspect sanitized error context, role/session identity, region, resource ARN, trust policy, identity/resource policies, explicit denies and encryption-key requirements. Use available audit logs and policy analysis tools. Compare local credentials with runtime role credentials and check expiry/assumption flow. Apply the smallest justified permission change and retest both allowed and denied cases.
questions.example: Local development uses an owner account while an ECS task uses a narrow task role. The runtime role can read an S3 object but cannot decrypt its KMS key. Granting unrelated EC2 permissions would not address the missing action.
questions.architecture: Runtime identity evidence -> denied action/resource -> applicable policy evaluation -> scoped correction -> allowed/denied integration checks -> audit
questions.metrics: Denied-request rate, least-privilege test coverage, unintended access attempts, recovery time and recurrence after credential rotation.
questions.tradeoffs: Detailed errors help diagnosis but must not disclose credentials or sensitive resource content. Temporary broad access often persists; prefer a reproducible narrow policy repair.
followups: Should you paste the access token into logs?
No. Log principal identifiers, request IDs and sanitized action/resource metadata needed for diagnosis, not raw credentials.
Could the error be networking instead?
Separate transport/connectivity failures from explicit authorization responses. Check request IDs and the actual service response before changing network or IAM settings.

quiz.prompt: Local owner credentials work, but the runtime task role gets AccessDenied. What should you inspect first?
options: The runtime principal and denied action/resource across applicable policies.
Grant administrator access to every service permanently.
Disable encryption for all stored data.
Change the UI font to reduce request size.

questions.title: Scenario: A patient-summary assistant confuses two patients with similar names. How do you repair the architecture?
questions.simple: Patient identity must come from a trusted application selection and authorization flow. The model must not infer identity from a name in free text.
questions.technical: Bind each request and retrieval query to a verified patient identifier and current user's permitted scope. Use source-level provenance and encounter timestamps, detect conflicting identifiers and stop ambiguous requests. Keep a human review path for clinical use. These are architecture exercises, not claims that this design alone satisfies legal or clinical requirements.
questions.example: Two patients named Alex Lee have different IDs. A summary request opened from patient A's chart must never search both charts by name similarity. A record with a conflicting patient ID should be rejected or quarantined before generation.
questions.architecture: Authenticated clinician -> trusted patient selection -> scoped record fetch -> identity/provenance validation -> grounded draft -> clinical review and audit
questions.metrics: Cross-patient retrieval rate, identity-conflict detection, critical-fact omissions, factual support and reviewer correction rate.
questions.tradeoffs: Failing closed on ambiguous identity interrupts workflow but protects a critical boundary. More fluent generation does not compensate for wrong-patient data.
followups: Would a prompt saying do not mix patients be enough?
No. Enforce patient scoping before retrieval and verify provenance independently of the model's text.
Should the assistant make autonomous treatment changes?
Not as a consequence of this summarization design. Clinical authority, review and validated scope must be defined separately.

quiz.prompt: Two patients share a name. What should scope a clinical summary's retrieval?
options: A verified patient ID from trusted application context and current authorization.
Only semantic name similarity.
The first chart the model remembers.
All matching records merged to maximize recall.

questions.title: Scenario: Two medical guideline documents conflict. Should RAG choose the newest one?
questions.simple: Recency is one clue, but applicability, authority, population and effective dates determine which evidence belongs to the case. Do not silently merge incompatible recommendations.
questions.technical: Store provenance, issuer, jurisdiction, effective/version dates and population scope. Retrieve applicable sources, surface conflicts, distinguish historical from current guidance and route unresolved material conflicts to an appropriate professional. RAG supports access to governed evidence; fine-tuning does not automatically resolve a changing clinical source hierarchy.
questions.example: A newer adult policy cannot automatically replace an older pediatric guideline for a child. The system must match population and setting before comparing dates.
questions.architecture: Case scope -> governed source catalog -> applicability filtering -> conflict-aware retrieval -> cited comparison -> professional escalation
questions.metrics: Applicability precision, outdated-source use, conflict detection and escalation accuracy, critical unsupported claims and reviewer agreement.
questions.tradeoffs: Stricter filters can miss relevant exceptions. Evaluate both missing applicable evidence and including harmful inapplicable material; uncertainty should be explicit.
followups: Why not fine-tune all guidelines into the model?
Updates and conflicting scopes need traceable evidence and source governance. Fine-tuning may improve task behavior but does not supply reliable current citations by itself.
Can the model rank clinical authority alone?
It can assist analysis, but authority and applicability rules should come from governed domain policy and professional oversight.

quiz.prompt: A newer adult guideline conflicts with an older pediatric guideline for a child. What matters first?
options: Applicable population, authority and effective scope before simple recency.
Always choose the document with the newest upload timestamp.
Merge both into one instruction without citing the conflict.
Raise temperature to choose randomly.

questions.title: Scenario: Threat intelligence in a retrieved page contains an instruction to disable logging. What should the SOC assistant do?
questions.simple: Threat reports are untrusted evidence, not operational commands. A report cannot grant itself permission to change security settings.
questions.technical: Separate extraction of indicators and claims from action authorization. Use trusted tool definitions, per-action permission checks, destination/resource allowlists and explicit review for high-impact changes. Preserve provenance and test indirect prompt-injection cases. A detector model can supplement controls but cannot replace server-side restrictions.
questions.example: A malicious report says run a command that disables audit collection before analyzing an indicator. The assistant can quote that text as suspicious evidence while the tool layer rejects any unauthorized configuration change.
questions.architecture: Untrusted feed -> isolated parsing and provenance -> evidence retrieval -> analyst-facing assessment -> policy-checked tools -> approved action and audit
questions.metrics: Unauthorized action rate, attack success rate, legitimate-task completion, analyst correction rate and tool-denial precision.
questions.tradeoffs: Restricting tools can slow response. Provide narrow approved actions and a clear escalation path rather than an unrestricted shell.
followups: Is read-only access harmless?
No. Unauthorized reads can disclose secrets through responses, caches or logs. Scope retrieval and output as well as writes.
Can a second agent approve every command?
It may help review but can share the same failure modes. Enforce permissions and high-impact approvals outside model text.

quiz.prompt: A threat report instructs the assistant to disable logs. What is the trust boundary?
options: Treat the report as data; independently authorize any tool action.
Treat retrieved text as a system instruction.
Disable logs because the report sounds technical.
Allow all shell commands if a second model agrees.

questions.title: Scenario: A SOC detector generates 20,000 alerts per day but analysts can review 500. How do you prioritize?
questions.simple: Optimize for useful investigations under a real review budget. Detecting everything is not operational success if important cases disappear in a backlog.
questions.technical: Deduplicate correlated events, enrich with asset criticality and trustworthy threat context, group incidents and rank by severity/likelihood/impact. Calibrate thresholds on representative labeled data and track selection bias from reviewed cases. Keep deterministic escalation rules for defined critical conditions. LLM summaries can aid triage without becoming the authoritative detector.
questions.example: One noisy endpoint produces 5,000 near-identical alerts. Group them into a single incident with event counts and time range, while preserving evidence and escalating a distinct high-impact event on a critical asset.
questions.architecture: Event intake -> deduplication and correlation -> risk scoring -> capacity-aware priority queue -> analyst investigation -> reviewed-label feedback
questions.metrics: Precision at review capacity, critical-event recall, time to triage, backlog age, duplicate compression and missed-incident severity.
questions.tradeoffs: Aggressive grouping can hide distinct attacks. Preserve underlying events and evaluate whether grouping merges unrelated incidents or suppresses rare high-impact signals.
followups: Why is accuracy a weak target?
True negatives dominate many detection tasks. Precision at a fixed analyst budget and critical recall better reflect the workflow's constraints.
How do you learn from unreviewed alerts?
Do not treat unreviewed as benign. Use delayed confirmed outcomes and a designed sampling strategy to reduce feedback bias.

quiz.prompt: With capacity to review 500 alerts per day, which metric is directly useful?
options: Precision at that review budget, alongside critical-event recall.
Overall accuracy alone on a mostly benign dataset.
Number of generated paragraphs per alert.
Alert volume maximized without regard to backlog.

questions.title: Scenario: A financial assistant adds figures correctly but mixes currency and reporting periods. What changes?
questions.simple: Correct arithmetic on incompatible numbers still produces a wrong business answer. Units, entity, period and accounting meaning must travel with every value.
questions.technical: Retrieve structured values with currency, scale, effective period, entity, source and revision. Validate compatible operands before deterministic calculation, apply an explicit exchange-rate policy when permitted and produce traceable citations. Keep the LLM focused on interpretation and explanation; use typed calculations and business rules for authoritative totals.
questions.example: Adding USD 10 million for Q1 to EUR 8 million for an entire year is not a meaningful comparable total. First align scope and period, then use a documented exchange rate if conversion is part of the task.
questions.architecture: Authorized question -> scoped structured retrieval -> unit/period/entity validation -> deterministic calculation -> evidence-linked explanation -> review
questions.metrics: Numeric exactness, unit/period mismatch detection, source traceability, inappropriate aggregation rate and reviewer correction rate.
questions.tradeoffs: Strict validation may require clarification instead of a quick answer. Silent assumptions are fast but can create material misstatements.
followups: Why not let the LLM do all calculations?
Deterministic tools provide reproducible arithmetic and explicit types. The model can still misunderstand scope, so validate inputs before calling the tool.
What if two filings restate the same period?
Track revision and authority, preserve provenance and use the version required by the question. Surface a material restatement rather than counting both.

quiz.prompt: Before adding financial figures from two sources, what must you validate?
options: Compatible currency, scale, reporting period, entity and measure.
Only whether both values are valid floating-point numbers.
Only that both sources contain a currency symbol.
Whether temperature is below 0.5.

questions.title: Scenario: A fraud assistant explains a score. Is that the same as deciding a transaction should be blocked?
questions.simple: An explanation assistant, a risk model and a transaction decision service have different responsibilities. Natural-language confidence should not become a payment-blocking rule.
questions.technical: Use a validated risk model or rules for scoring and an authorized decision service for effects. Retrieve case evidence with timestamps, distinguish observed facts from hypotheses and expose reason codes faithfully. Apply review and appeal/escalation paths appropriate to the business. RAG provides evidence access; it is not automatically a calibrated fraud classifier.
questions.example: A high amount is unusual for one customer but normal for another. An assistant can summarize that context, while a policy-controlled decision layer combines calibrated risk, customer history and action thresholds.
questions.architecture: Transaction features -> validated risk score -> policy decision or review -> scoped evidence retrieval -> faithful investigator summary -> audited outcome
questions.metrics: Fraud loss, false-decline rate, precision/recall at threshold, calibration, explanation fidelity and review turnaround.
questions.tradeoffs: More conservative review can reduce false declines but increase delay and operational cost. Explain these costs separately from language-generation quality.
followups: Can a persuasive explanation make a poor score reliable?
No. It can conceal uncertainty. Evaluate scoring and explanatory faithfulness independently, including cases where evidence is weak.
What should the assistant do with missing evidence?
State the missing field or uncertainty and use the defined review path. Do not invent a causal story to fill a fluent paragraph.

quiz.prompt: Which component should authorize a transaction-blocking effect?
options: A policy-controlled decision service using validated inputs and permissions.
The assistant's prose confidence alone.
Any retrieved document mentioning fraud.
The highest-temperature generated explanation.

questions.title: Scenario: An e-commerce support agent must refund an order. Why not expose arbitrary SQL?
questions.simple: A refund is a specific business operation with eligibility and authorization rules. A narrow refund API can enforce them better than unrestricted database access.
questions.technical: Bind the request to authenticated ownership, check order state and refund policy, calculate the permitted amount deterministically and require the appropriate confirmation/approval. Use an idempotency key and reconcile uncertain payment outcomes. Retrieve policy explanations separately from the effectful refund operation.
questions.example: If the customer repeats a request after a timeout, the same logical refund operation should return its recorded status. A new unrestricted SQL write or new payment ID could create a second refund.
questions.architecture: Authenticated order selection -> current policy and order checks -> approved refund intent -> idempotent payment API -> durable status -> confirmation
questions.metrics: Unauthorized/duplicate refund rate, eligibility correctness, reconciliation lag, completion rate and customer wait time.
questions.tradeoffs: Narrow APIs need deliberate endpoint development. They reduce flexibility but make permissions, invariants and audit much clearer than a generic shell or write-SQL tool.
followups: Can retrieved policy text authorize a refund?
No. The trusted backend enforces the approved policy and current order/user state. Retrieval supplies explanatory evidence, not authority.
Does a timeout mean the refund failed?
No. Reconcile the provider's original operation before deciding whether to retry or escalate.

quiz.prompt: A refund request times out after reaching the payment service. What should happen next?
options: Reconcile the original idempotent operation before retrying.
Issue a new refund immediately with a new ID.
Assume no money moved because the UI timed out.
Give the model direct owner-level SQL credentials.

questions.title: Scenario: A legal contract assistant retrieves the right clause but misses an exception. How do you improve it?
questions.simple: A clause can depend on definitions, cross-references and amendments. Retrieve the necessary surrounding evidence and expose uncertainty instead of presenting a legal conclusion as certain.
questions.technical: Preserve document hierarchy, clause IDs, definitions, amendment precedence and parties/effective dates. Retrieve parent/linked clauses when justified, trace every substantive claim to spans and evaluate exceptions/negation explicitly. Use qualified review for consequential interpretation. Adding all documents to context can bury the exception and exceed the token budget.
questions.example: A termination clause says 30 days' notice except for a defined breach event elsewhere. A summary that quotes only the 30-day sentence is supported locally but incomplete for the actual question.
questions.architecture: Authorized contract set -> clause and cross-reference retrieval -> applicability/amendment checks -> claim-level draft -> exception validation -> reviewer
questions.metrics: Exception recall, citation support/completeness, wrong-party/version rate, unsupported conclusions and reviewer correction burden.
questions.tradeoffs: Expanding context raises latency and distraction. Use targeted cross-reference retrieval and a stopping rule, then escalate unresolved ambiguity.
followups: Does a citation prove the complete answer is correct?
No. A citation can support one sentence while missing a material exception. Evaluate completeness and applicability as well as support.
Why not fine-tune instead of RAG?
Contract-specific and amended facts need traceable current evidence. Fine-tuning can improve extraction behavior but does not replace access-controlled source lookup.

quiz.prompt: A termination answer omits a cross-referenced exception. What should retrieval preserve?
options: Clause links, definitions, amendments and applicable surrounding evidence.
Only the highest-scoring isolated sentence.
Only vector distance without document identity.
A fixed answer memorized during fine-tuning.

questions.title: Scenario: A frontend release works for some users but others load stale JavaScript. How do you deploy safely?
questions.simple: The HTML and its referenced assets must form a compatible release. Browser/CDN caching can mix versions if filenames and cache rules are poorly designed.
questions.technical: Use content-hashed immutable assets, short-lived or revalidated entry HTML, atomic deployments and versioned API contracts. Check service-worker behavior if present, actual request URLs, cache headers and error telemetry. Distinguish a cached old page from a new deployment missing files. Keep rollback assets available for the required compatibility window.
questions.example: An old index references app-old.js that was deleted during deployment. A user with cached HTML gets a blank page even though a fresh load works. Retaining versioned assets and controlling entry-point caching avoids this mixed release.
questions.architecture: Versioned build -> hashed assets and compatible API -> atomic publish -> HTML revalidation -> client error monitoring -> rollback
questions.metrics: Asset 404 rate, startup error rate, version distribution, successful page initialization and rollback recovery time.
questions.tradeoffs: Long asset retention costs storage; overly aggressive no-cache on every asset slows repeat visits. Cache immutable assets separately from the mutable entry document.
followups: Does hard refresh fix every user's architecture?
It can confirm a cache symptom but is not a deployment design. Correct versioning and headers so ordinary users recover automatically.
Should source credentials enter the frontend bundle?
No. Runtime credentials remain in the backend/Function environment; public build output is readable by visitors.

quiz.prompt: Which release design reduces stale HTML referencing missing JavaScript?
options: Hashed assets, revalidated entry HTML and compatible atomic deployment.
Delete old assets immediately and cache index forever.
Put database credentials in the browser to fetch new code.
Tell every user to reinstall their operating system.

questions.title: Scenario: Two users edit the same record and one change disappears. How do you prevent lost updates?
questions.simple: A write should detect whether someone changed the record after it was read. Do not silently overwrite a newer revision with an older copy.
questions.technical: Use optimistic concurrency with a revision/version or ETag and an atomic compare-and-set update. A mismatch returns a conflict so the client can reload or merge intentionally. Transactions and appropriate isolation/locking can handle stronger invariants. Keep idempotency of retried requests separate from detecting competing edits.
questions.example: Both clients read revision 7. Client A writes revision 8. Client B submits expected revision 7 and must receive a conflict rather than overwrite A. PrepAtoZ uses revision checks for account progress.
questions.architecture: Read record and revision -> client edit -> conditional atomic update -> success with new revision or conflict -> deliberate merge
questions.metrics: Lost-update incidents, conflict rate, successful conflict resolution, write latency and retry amplification.
questions.tradeoffs: Optimistic concurrency works well when conflicts are uncommon. High-contention workflows may need serialization or domain-specific merges rather than endless conflict retries.
followups: Can the client compare versions before sending and guarantee safety?
No. Another write can occur between comparison and update. The server/database must enforce the condition atomically.
Can you merge every JSON field automatically?
Not safely. Notes, counters and state transitions have different semantics; use a domain-defined merge or ask for resolution.

quiz.prompt: Two clients read revision 7. One saves revision 8. What should the other's revision-7 write do?
options: Fail with a conflict unless a deliberate safe merge is applied.
Silently overwrite revision 8.
Always succeed because both users are authenticated.
Reset all other users' sessions.

questions.title: Scenario: Login succeeds but API calls still return unauthorized. What do you inspect?
questions.simple: Check whether the browser actually received and sent the intended session cookie. Authentication also depends on domain, path, HTTPS and server-side session validity.
questions.technical: Inspect sanitized network status and Set-Cookie/Cookie behavior, SameSite, Secure, expiry, request credentials mode, origin and session lookup. Check server time and shared database configuration across instances. Do not log raw session tokens or weaken CSRF checks to hide a cookie issue. Cross-origin deployment requires an explicit supported credential/CORS design.
questions.example: A frontend on one origin calls another without the required credential mode, so no cookie accompanies /api/progress. A successful login response alone does not prove subsequent requests carry an authenticated session.
questions.architecture: Login response -> cookie acceptance -> authenticated request context -> shared session lookup -> expiry/role validation -> authorized API
questions.metrics: Login-to-session continuity, unauthorized rate after login, cookie rejection causes, session-store latency and successful logout invalidation.
questions.tradeoffs: Broad cross-site cookie settings increase complexity and exposure. A same-origin API simplifies deployment, but every mutation still needs appropriate CSRF protection.
followups: Should you move the session token into localStorage to bypass the problem?
Not as an automatic fix. It changes the threat model and exposure to script access. Diagnose the cookie contract and preserve appropriate HttpOnly handling.
Why can one server accept the user while another rejects them?
They may use different secrets/stores, clocks or configuration. Use shared durable session state and consistent runtime configuration.

quiz.prompt: Login responds successfully but the next API request has no cookie. What is the first boundary to inspect?
options: Cookie acceptance and request credential/domain/path/SameSite behavior.
The model's embedding dimension.
Whether the password hash is displayed in the UI.
Disabling all authorization checks permanently.

questions.title: Scenario: Your LLM provider is slow or unavailable. How should the application degrade?
questions.simple: Set time budgets and define which useful features can still work. An unbounded queue or endless retry loop only makes an outage larger.
questions.technical: Use per-call deadlines within an end-to-end budget, bounded retries for classified transient failures, circuit breaking where appropriate and admission control. Provide a cited retrieved-evidence view or deferred job if it meets the task. Any fallback model must pass required quality, security and data-handling constraints; never silently downgrade a critical guarantee.
questions.example: During an outage, a policy assistant can show authorized source passages with a clear generation-unavailable message. A payment agent must not fabricate a successful action or move to an unapproved endpoint.
questions.architecture: Request deadline and admission -> primary inference -> bounded retry/circuit policy -> evaluated fallback or evidence-only response -> incident telemetry
questions.metrics: Successful task completion, fallback correctness, timeout rate, queue age, retry load, recovery time and cost per useful response.
questions.tradeoffs: A second provider improves resilience only if quotas, data rules and failure domains differ. Extra dependencies and inconsistent behavior can outweigh availability gains.
followups: Should every failed request be retried three times?
No. Classify failures, honor total deadlines and account for idempotency and load. Invalid requests and denied permissions need correction rather than repetition.
Is an evidence-only response always safe?
No. The evidence must still be authorized, applicable and clearly presented without implying an evaluated generated conclusion.

quiz.prompt: The generation provider is unavailable. Which fallback is defensible for a policy assistant?
options: An explicitly labeled view of authorized evidence, if useful and supported by the task.
Fabricating an answer so the UI never shows an error.
Retrying forever without a deadline.
Sending confidential data to any unapproved provider.

questions.title: Scenario: Retrieval finds the correct document but the wrong section. Is increasing top-k enough?
questions.simple: A document match does not mean the exact evidence reached the model. Inspect the retrieved chunks and the assembled prompt, not just the file title.
questions.technical: Evaluate chunk-level relevance, section hierarchy, exact terms, metadata filters, reranking and context packing. Try parent/adjacent or cross-reference expansion with a token budget when required evidence spans boundaries. Use labeled query-to-span examples and compare changes independently. Increasing k can improve recall while adding noise and burying the answer.
questions.example: A cancellation question retrieves a 200-page policy's introduction but not its cancellation exception. Recover the relevant clause through better chunk boundaries, keyword/hybrid matching or focused section retrieval, then verify it survives prompt assembly.
questions.architecture: Query and scope -> hybrid candidates -> chunk-level rerank -> targeted hierarchy expansion -> token-budgeted context -> grounded answer
questions.metrics: Evidence-span recall@k, context precision, exception coverage, end-answer correctness, token cost and p95 latency.
questions.tradeoffs: Parent expansion improves context but adds unrelated text. Tune on long/short documents and exception-heavy questions rather than only average cases.
followups: Could the reranker still fail?
Yes. Its training/task fit, truncation and input formatting can hide the critical span. Log candidates and scores and evaluate its added value separately.
Why not fine-tune the whole policy corpus?
It weakens source/update traceability for changing facts. Fine-tuning can improve behavior while governed retrieval supplies applicable evidence.

quiz.prompt: A correct document's irrelevant introduction is retrieved for an exception question. What should you measure?
options: Chunk/evidence-span recall and whether the required clause reaches the prompt.
Only document filename match rate.
Only whether top-k is larger than ten.
Only the number of model parameters.

questions.title: Scenario: Query rewriting improves retrieval but changes the user's intent. How do you constrain it?
questions.simple: A rewrite should make the search clearer while preserving entities, constraints and uncertainty. It must not silently invent a different question.
questions.technical: Retain the original query, use typed extraction for critical constraints and validate entity/date/negation preservation. Search original and rewritten variants where beneficial, deduplicate and rerank evidence, and ask for clarification when ambiguity is material. Log both versions and evaluate semantic drift on labeled difficult cases. Do not let a rewrite expand authorization scope.
questions.example: 'Which orders are not refundable after 14 days?' must not become 'refundable orders within 14 days.' Losing negation reverses the requested answer even if retrieval scores improve.
